Scion

SY-un · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Scion is a descendant of a notable, wealthy, or influential family; also (in gardening) a plant shoot used for grafting.

As the scion of one of the city's oldest banking families, she felt enormous pressure to take over the business herself.

Worked Example

The scion of the shipping dynasty surprised everyone by walking away from the family business to become a schoolteacher instead.

A scion often carries an expectation -- of continuing a family's wealth, name, or business -- whether or not they want that role.

How Scion Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

heir

heir: a person legally entitled to inherit property, a title, or a position

descendant

descendant: a person descended from a particular ancestor or family

Antonyms

ancestor

ancestor: a person from whom one is descended

predecessor

predecessor: someone who came before, in a role or lineage

How Strong Is It? — relative → heir apparent → scion

relative vs. scion

relative vs. scion: A relative is any family member, without implying inherited status or wealth.

heir apparent vs. scion

heir apparent vs. scion: An heir apparent is the person certain and next in line to inherit a title or position -- even more specific than a general scion.

Build the Word

The pieces

whole word (no suffix) — scion

whole word (no suffix) — scion: borrowed whole from Old French cion/sion, meaning 'a shoot or twig of a plant' -- there is no separate root here; the -ion at the end is a coincidence of spelling, not this unit's suffix (Old French)

Put it together

Put it together: Scion is this unit's flagged false friend: unlike the other 14 words here, it was NOT built from a root plus the -ion suffix. It came into English whole, from Old French cion (a plant shoot), and later extended to mean a family's descendant -- as if a person were a new shoot growing from an old family tree.

Where it comes from

Where it comes from: Scion was borrowed whole from Old French cion, 'a young shoot or twig' -- the -ion at its end is a spelling coincidence, not this unit's suffix. Calling an heir a scion pictures the person as a fresh green shoot growing from the old family tree.

Strength Check

Word Choice

Scion sounds like it should decompose with the -ion suffix, but it doesn't -- see the note on the lead card. Use it for a notable family's descendant, often with a hint of privilege or expectation attached to the name.
